clinicalPearls: C8 is a terminal complement component that triggers C9 polymerisation, so its deficiency impairs membrane attack complex formation and predisposes to recurrent neisserial infection.
The protein has three chains (alpha, beta and gamma); deficiency of the alpha-gamma subunit is more frequent in some populations while beta-chain deficiency predominates in others.
Recurrent meningococcal disease, often with uncommon serogroups, is the characteristic clinical picture and mirrors C6 and C7 deficiency.
CH50/CH100 is profoundly low or undetectable and AH50 is abnormal, reflecting a block at a component shared by both terminal pathways.
Disseminated gonococcal infection can also occur and should prompt consideration of a terminal complement defect.
Invasive infection typically begins in later childhood or adolescence and may recur, though episodes are often less fatal than in the general population.
Meningococcal (including serogroup B and conjugate) and other encapsulated-organism vaccines, plus prompt treatment of fever, are the mainstays of care.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive; the causative gene depends on the subunit involved (C8A or C8G for the alpha-gamma defect, C8B for the beta-chain defect).
reference.pathophysiology: Complement Component 8 deficiency is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants affecting the C8 molecule, which is composed of three chains: an alpha-gamma dimer encoded by C8A and C8G and a separately encoded beta chain from C8B. Within the terminal cascade, C8 binds the membrane-inserted C5b-7 complex and its alpha chain initiates the recruitment and polymerisation of multiple C9 molecules that form the lytic transmembrane channel of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9). Loss of functional C8 therefore prevents completion of the MAC and abolishes complement-mediated direct killing of Gram-negative bacteria, while upstream opsonic and anaphylatoxin functions remain intact. As with other terminal defects, this selectively cripples serum bactericidal activity against Neisseria species, producing susceptibility to invasive meningococcal disease and disseminated gonococcal infection. Two genetically distinct forms exist: alpha-gamma subunit deficiency (variants in C8A or C8G) and beta subunit deficiency (variants in C8B), with differing population frequencies but a shared clinical phenotype. Immunity outside the terminal complement pathway is otherwise normal.
additionalDifferentials: C6 deficiency with the same neisserial susceptibility
C7 deficiency, clinically indistinguishable without component assay
C5 deficiency, which also impairs chemotaxis via C5a
C9 deficiency, usually a milder terminal defect
Properdin deficiency causing X-linked fulminant meningococcaemia
Primary antibody deficiency with recurrent encapsulated bacterial infection
additionalInvestigations: CH50/CH100 haemolytic complement assay as the initial screen
AH50 alternative-pathway assay to localise a terminal-component block
Specific C8 antigenic and functional levels, distinguishing alpha-gamma from beta deficiency
Sequencing of C8A, C8B and C8G to identify the causative subunit and variant
Blood and cerebrospinal fluid culture with meningococcal serogrouping in acute disease
Measurement of the other terminal components to exclude combined deficiency
Haemolytic complement screening of first-degree relatives
redFlags: Neisserial infection due to an uncommon serogroup
Family history of recurrent or fatal meningococcal infection
Fever, headache, neck stiffness or purpuric rash in a known C8-deficient patient
Repeatedly undetectable CH50/CH100 outside an acute consumptive state
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally good with vaccination, patient education and rapid antimicrobial treatment of acute episodes, and invasive neisserial disease in affected patients tends to carry a lower case-fatality than in the wider population. Recurrent infection is the principal enduring risk and justifies lifelong preventive measures.
pitfalls: Not screening the complement system after invasive neisserial infection, especially with rare serogroups or recurrence.
Measuring only total C8 without distinguishing alpha-gamma from beta-chain deficiency, which can obscure the genetic diagnosis.
Accepting a low CH50 from a poorly handled specimen as a genuine deficiency.
Assuming vaccines eliminate risk and relaxing clinical vigilance for breakthrough infection.
Omitting family counselling and screening after a proband is diagnosed.
references: Standard clinical immunology textbook, current edition
National immunisation guidance for complement-deficient and asplenic patients
Peer-reviewed reviews of terminal complement deficiency and neisserial disease
management: Vaccinate against meningococcus with quadrivalent conjugate (ACWY) and serogroup B vaccines, maintaining boosters, to offset absent membrane-attack-complex killing.
Keep pneumococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b immunisation current.
Treat febrile illness promptly with empirical antibiotics covering Neisseria and confirm the serogroup microbiologically.
Consider prophylactic penicillin for those with recurrent meningococcal disease.
Educate patient and family in recognising meningococcal illness and provide an emergency treatment plan.
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and screen relatives for terminal-complement deficiency.
